title: School voucher program on student test scores

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy

The appropriate causal method for this research question is a **Difference-in-Differences (DID)** design. This is suitable because we have panel data (multiple periods for the same units) with a clearly defined treatment group (districts receiving the voucher program) and a control group (districts not receiving the program), and a specific exogeneous intervention period (period 4).

The core idea of DID is to compare the change in test scores over time for the treated districts to the change over the same period for the control districts. This approach helps to control for both time-invariant differences between treated and control districts and common time trends affecting all districts.

The key assumption for the validity of the DID estimator is the **Parallel Trends Assumption**. This assumption states that, in the absence of the voucher program, the average trend in test scores for the treated districts would have been the same as the average trend for the control districts. In other words, any pre-existing differences in trends between the two groups would need to be accounted for, or assumed to be zero. With district and period fixed effects, the model implicitly accounts for fixed differences between districts and common shocks over time, strengthening the plausibility of the parallel trends assumption after controlling for these factors.

## 2. R Code

```r
# Install and load necessary packages
if (!requireNamespace("fixest", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("fixest")
}
if (!requireNamespace("data.table", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("data.table")
}
library(fixest)
library(data.table)

# Define the file path
data_path <- "experiments/exp_b/data/s03_data.csv"

# Read the data
# Using data.table::fread for efficiency with larger files
df <- fread(data_path)

# Ensure unit_id and period are treated as factors for fixed effects
df[, unit_id := as.factor(unit_id)]
df[, period := as.factor(period)]

# Implement the Difference-in-Differences regression
# Model: y = beta_0 + beta_1 * treat_x_post + beta_2 * treated + beta_3 * post + unit_id FE + period FE + epsilon
# The coefficient of interest is beta_1 (on treat_x_post)
# We include fixed effects for unit_id to control for all time-invariant district-specific unobservables
# We include fixed effects for period to control for all time-specific common shocks

# Basic DID model with unit and time fixed effects
# Standard errors clustered by unit_id are crucial for panel data to account for within-unit correlation
did_model <- feols(y ~ treat_x_post + treated + post | unit_id + period,
                   data = df,
                   cluster = ~unit_id)

# Print the regression results
cat("--- DID Regression Results ---\n")
print(etable(did_model, fitstat = c('n', 'r2'), title = "DID Model: Voucher Program Impact on Test Scores"))

# Robustness Check: Re-run the model with standard errors clustered by both unit_id and period (two-way clustering)
# This accounts for potential correlation both within districts over time and within periods across districts
did_model_robust_cluster <- feols(y ~ treat_x_post + treated + post | unit_id + period,
                                  data = df,
                                  cluster = ~unit_id + period)

cat("\n--- DID Regression Results (Two-way Clustered Std Errors) ---\n")
print(etable(did_model_robust_cluster, fitstat = c('n', 'r2'), title = "DID Model (Two-way Clustered SEs)"))

# Extract and print the key coefficient (impact of voucher program)
did_coeff <- coef(did_model)["treat_x_post"]
did_se <- se(did_model)["treat_x_post"]
cat(sprintf("\nEstimated impact of voucher program (treat_x_post): %.4f (SE: %.4f)\n", did_coeff, did_se))
```

## 3. Expected Findings

Given that the research question investigates whether the introduction of a school voucher program "improved" standardized test scores, one would **expect a positive sign** for the coefficient on `treat_x_post`. The underlying economic theory suggests that voucher programs, by introducing competition among schools and giving parents more choices, could incentivize schools to improve their quality, leading to better student outcomes. Alternatively, if students in voucher programs move to higher-quality private schools, their scores might increase.

The **magnitude** of the coefficient will depend on the scaling of the standardized test scores (`y`). Since `y` is mean-centered, a positive coefficient of, say, 0.1 would imply that the voucher program increased test scores in treated districts by 0.1 standard deviations compared to the counterfactual (what would have happened without the program, relative to control districts). A "meaningful" magnitude would typically be in the range of 0.05 to 0.25 standard deviations, as often seen in education interventions. A coefficient close to zero or negative would suggest that the program had no significant positive impact, or even a detrimental one.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: DID — treated=voucher districts, control=non-voucher; shock=program introduction
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Test scores increase significantly in voucher districts after program launch
